The proposed change is to transfer the Department of Landscape Architecture from the
College of Arts and Sciences to the College of the Environment and Life Sciences. The
transfer will result in the relocation of a design program that offers an accredited BLA and
educates students about profession of landscape architecture and focuses many of its
project assignments on addressing issues of community and urban design, sustainable
design and coastal resilience, and ecological and environmental design and planning. At
any given moment, the average number of students in the department averages between
55 and 70. It should be noted that our sophomore class is typically filled and capped at 20.
Our average graduating class of is 16.6 over 10 years. LAR will also bring to the college an
existing Graduate Certificate in Community Planning, minors in both CPL and LAR and the
desire to create a new master's program. This relocation will strengthen the college by
adding a design unit with visualization capabilities and a track record for collaborative
problem-solving and award-winning service-learning studio project. The move will
enhance LAR'S positioning for research, and it will make it easier to collaborate with the
existing college's disciplines, many of which are addressing the same issues. In addition,
faculty in LAR and CELS are already involved in interdisciplinary exchanges through team

B1. Why is the new program being developed?
The Harrington core curriculum was approved and developed by the faculty to ensure
that all Harrington School graduates have a shared set of essential skills from across the
contemporary communication and media landscape. The core curriculum reflects the
unique contributions that each program makes to our understanding of communication
and media. Beyond fulfilling many of the core requirements in general education, the
Harrington core will provide our students with the unique opportunity to develop and
enhance their digital media production skills via the Production and Presentation
Fundamentals (SCM 105) requirement; competencies that are essential and applicable
across a wide variety of industries and careers. Lastly, the core curriculum recognizes
the value of interdisciplinary education for all Harrington students.

students in each of the 6 undergraduate majors currently offered under the Harrington
School of Communication: Communication Studies, Film Studies, Journalism, Public

Rationale:URI's‘Second Grade Option'(UM$8.33.32;SGO hereafter) currently
allows students at the beginning of their URI career to retake courses in which they received a C-
or below. Doing so requires that they get approval from their academic dean and submit a form
totheOfficeofEnrollmentServiceseach timetheyintendtoemploytheSGO.After they've
done so, the original grade remains on their transcript but is not used in QPA calculations.
AmongcomparableNewEnglandpublicinstitutions,URIalonerestrictsthetimeframe
for course repeats and requires the submission of additional paperwork. Within Rhode Island,
Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island allow any course to be
repeated and automatically use the second grade earned in a course in GPA calculations. Similar
policies can be found at other New England public universities (UCONN, UNH, UMASS, UVM,
UMaine). URI itself temporarily expanded use of the SGO during the COVID-19 pandemic in
2020but reverted to the existingpolicy afterwards.
Using longitudinal administrative data from a four-year public institution that alternated
between two grading schemes over a short period of seven years, Jiang et al. (2021) found that
the adoption of the grade forgiveness policy, over the traditional practice of grade averaging,
nudges students to pursue curriculum and/or degrees perceived as relatively more challenging
and/or with harder grading standards, such as those in Science, Technology, Engineering, and
Mathematics (STEM). They also found no evidence that grade forgiveness delayed graduation or
reducedstudenteffort.
Contention aroundexcessivecourserepetitionmaycausesignificantdisruptions to a
student outcomes such as time to degree completion (Jiang et al. 2021; Marx & Meeler 2013).
The latter study also reports that grade forgiveness may also place an unforeseen social or
financial burden on students and create challenges with course enrollment.These arguments,
along with others, are ultimately empirical questions that prior work has not fully addressed and
canbeuniquetospecificinstitutions.
Considerations to change grade forgiveness policies can affect student achievement and
propensities to explore and experiment with different majors, and as a result, may have a
substantial impact on the distribution of desirable majors and career fields that are increasingly in
high demand (Jiang et al.2021; Stinebrickner & Stinebrickner2014).Morel(2023) foundhidden
and“credential cartels”that limit thenumber ofunderrepresented students incertain majors
based on GPA requirements and “secondary admissions processes." Jiang et al. (2021) found that

Program (hereinafter to be referred to as the “Graduate Program'), as described herein and to be
delivered in accordance with the terms and obligations of this Agreement and the Scope of Work
in Appendix 1 attached hereto.
II.
COMMENCEMENT
This Agreement shall commence on August 31, 2022 and shall be automatically
renewed each year upon the anniversary of said commencement date (the “Renewal Date') and
shall continue for a maximum of ten (1o) years, unless sooner terminated by either party in
accordance with the terms herein. Upon expiration of the Agreement, any additional term
extensions shall be mutually agreed upon in writing by the parties. Either party may terminate
this Agreement by serving upon the other party a written notice, of not less than 90 days, in
advance of the Renewal Date.
IH.
INSURANCE, INDEMNIFICATION and LIMITATION OF LIABILITY
Insurance
Throughout the entire term of the Agreement, each party shall maintain commercial
general liability insurance covering their activities under this Agreement, in amounts of at least
One Million Dollars ($1,000,000) per incident and Two Million Dollars ($2,000,000) in the
coverage via electronic (email) distribution to an address designated by University.
All students participating in the Graduate Program who are enrolled as students at the
University will be covered by the University's aforementioned commercial liability insurance.
All students participating in the Graduate Program who are also employed by Sodexo, or
obtaining supervised experiential learning in dietetics provided by Sodexo shall likewise be
covered by Sodexo's aforementioned commercial liability insurance.

negligence or wrongful conduct of the University or any of its employees, agents, representatives

SODEXOPERSONNEL
participate in the Graduate Program and the supervised experiential learning in dietetics provided

V.
ASSIGNMENTANDGOVERNINGLAW
This Agreement or any part thereof shall not be assigned without the prior written
consent of the other party. Any attempted assignment without the aforementioned consent shall
render this Agreement null and void.

State of Rhode Island, without regard for that state's choice of law principles.

DISCRIMINATION
No person shall, on the grounds of race, color, sex, religion, sexual orientation,

CONFIDENTIALITY

Brief Descriptionof the GraduateProgram
The Graduate Program will be accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in
Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND) to provide the education and experiential learning
requirements for students to become Registered Dietitians. URI will provide the didactic
requirements culminating in a MS degree in Dietetics, and Sodexo will provide the required
minimum of 1,000 hours of supervised experiential learning.
Responsibilities of the University of Rhode Island
The responsibilities of the University of Rhode Island are to:
Provide the Graduate Program Director who meets the requirements of URI and the
Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND). The Graduate
Program Director will have a 50% time allocation to administer the Graduate Program. The
Graduate Program Director will be responsible for overall management of the Graduate
Program following ACEND and URI guidelines.
Provide all of the responsibilities required in the ACEND Standards for a Graduate Program
Provide all didactic and practicum courses and course instructors (with the exception of the
required “supervised experiential learning” activities to be provided by Sodexo in connection
with their own independent, longstanding “Dietetic Internship Program", and as described
below) for the Graduate Program culminating in a MS degree in Dietetics and fulfilling
ACEND competencies. A minimum of 75% of the student's time or credit hours will be at
the University.
·Confer the degree and maintain student records.
· Provide the ACEND verification statement upon Graduate Program completion and maintain
these statements indefinitely.
·Assess prior learning of students upon entry to the Graduate Program.
· Provide the resources needed to offer the MS degree including administrative/clerical
support, IT support, facilities, and student support services.
Develop and market the Graduate Program to potential students.
Share data with the Sodexo co-Director, following FERPA guidelines, to ensure that students
successfully complete the experiential learning component of the Graduate Program and to
submit accreditation documentation.
Responsibilitiesof theSodexoCorporation
The responsibilities of the Sodexo Corporation are to:
· Provide the Graduate Program Co-Director to manage supervised experiential learning.
·Provide preceptors for supervised experiential learning.
Provide a minimum of 1,0o0 hours of supervised experiential learning activities for each
student to meet ACEND competencies.
Provide the resources needed for supervised experiential learning including
administrative/clerical support, IT support, facilities, and student support services.
Participate in writing of all ACEND required reports.
Share data with the Graduate Program Director, following FERPA guidelines, to ensure that
the Graduate Program can assign grades, confer degrees, and submit accreditation
documentation.
Other requirements set forth in the Affiliation Agreement
Have full legal and administrative responsibility for all aspects of the supervised experiential
learning in dietetics at Sodexo, including responsibility for the collection of all Sodexo
tuition and other fees from students, and the maintenance of all appropriate policies and
procedures for the experiential learning, and adherence to all applicable laws, including
federal and state labor laws, relating to the supervised experiential learning in dietetics at

·Each Collaborating Organization will charge its own tuition and fees, and this money will be
used to pay its individual costs. Neither Collaborating Organization is responsible for paying

Each Collaborating Organization will equally share in the accreditation fees (annual fee and

TeachOutProcess
If the Graduate Program is dissolved, or the Affiliation Agreement is terminated by either party,
the Collaborating Organizations agree to teach out any students remaining in the Graduate

Program length. Since the Graduate Program length is 14 months, the teach out process will be
concludedby 21months.

Iam writing to designate you, as Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences, the interim authority
responsible for the oversight of the Center forPeace and Nonviolence at The University of Rhode Island.
In that role, you will replace the Provost as the authority overseeing the Center. In that role, please
appoint an Interim Director and oversee the facuity senate process to formally transfer the responsibility
for the Center from the Office of the Provost to the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences. In this
designee role, you will have overall responsibility for the Center and its budgets. The Interim Director, and
ultimately the Director, will have responsibility for managing the operations, programs, and staff of the
Center. The Interim Director will report to you as the designated authority for the Center.
Center History and Purpose
My understanding is that the Center for Nonviolence & Peace Studies was given permanent status as a
"Center" in 2002 and has reported through the Provost Office since that time. The Center continues to be
an important component for study and activism at the University of Rhode Island. Asyouknow,we have
begun working through the faculty senateprocess to transfer the responsibility for and the location of the
Center from the Provost Office to the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences. In addition, our intention
is to transfer the existing budget and also the course code relating to any existing or future courses
offered by the Center. However, until review and approval by the faculty senate has been completed, 1
ask that you serve as my designee responsible as the reporting authority for the Center and its Director.
Assuming positive action by fhe faculty senate at some future date, the Center will then be officially
relocated within the College of Arts and Sciences, although faculty and student involvement should
continue to span colleges and departments at the university in keeping with the decidedly interdisciplinary
purpose of the Center articulated when it was established. As articulated in the original Center proposal,
which was supported by the College of Arts and Sciences Curriculum Committee, the Center is “an
interdisciplinary partnership for research, teaching, and outreach related to nonviolence and peace
studies as applied to individual and community development, conflict resolution and reconciliation, and
constructive social change. A notable feature of the URl Center is the joining together of academic
accomplishments of nonviolent leadership and social change of the past century, such as those of Gandhi
and Martin Luther King Jr."
The statedmission of the Center isas follows:"To institutionalizeand internationalize nonviolenceas a
transformative educational process that reduces human suffering and promotes a global beloved
community; to foster mutual understanding among people, in which nonviolent processes are used to
reconcileconflicts andtobuildpeacefulsustainable,andinclusivecommunities;to collaboratewithand
strengthenrelationships with other organizations,agencies,and governmental departments engaged in
peacebuilding and nonviolence work at the local, national, and global levels; and fo accomplish this
mission, the Centerfor Nonviolence &Peace Studies organizes and provides training and education
opportunities forindividuals,organizations,and communifies seeking to engage in the fundamental study
ofnonviolenceandpeaceful alternativestoconflictandviolence."
I appreciate your willingness to take on this additional responsibility. Please let me know if you have
questions, Thank you.

Rationale: URI's “Second Grade Option' (UM S8.33.32; SGO hereafter) allows students
at the beginning of their URI career to retake courses in which they received a C- or below.
When they do so, the original grade remains on their transcript but is not used in QPA
calculations. The only exception to this rule occurs when determining whether students are
eligible to graduate with distinction (≥3.3 cum laude, ≥3.5 magna cum laude, ≥3.7 summa cum
laude). The QPA to determine eligibility for this honor is calculated using ALL courses taken at
the university, including any repeated using the SGO, rather than the QPA printed on the
student's transcript. This results in some students who exercised the SGO being ineligible for
honors despite having a suitable QPA. on their transcript.
The argument for the current approach is comparing two students with the same QPA,
one of whom exercised their rights to a SGO and the other who did not, the latter student is more
deserving of graduation with distinction than the former. Put another way, students wishing to
graduate with distinction should be held to a ‘higher standard' than the transcript-listed QPA.
Jack Humphrey, the registrar, notes, “My research regarding the history of including all
courses alttempted at the University dates back to the 70's. There was a concern that by not
counting all attempts, academic honors could be awarded on an unequal basis (those that
utilized the 2nd grade option could be given the academic honors as students that did not have
any courses that qualified for the 2nd grade option). In addition, since the 2nd grade option is
not mandatory, it could disenfranchise students who chose to not exercise the 2nd grade option
who would have otherwise qualified for academic honors had they chosen to use the 2nd grade
option at the start of their undergraduate academic career
My concern if we were to eliminate calculating distinction without taking into account all
course attempts would be that distinction at commencement would become less meaningful."
There was also concern changing the current policy might affect students who, although
initially dismissed from URI for poor grades, significantly improved their academic performance
after being readmitted under the ^conditional readmission' program (UM $8.25.13 - 8.25.16).
the policy might increase their chances of earning this distinction.
There are two arguments against the current approach. First, both the SGO and
conditional readmission program provide a measure of forgiveness for mistakes made early in a
student's career; the same principle should apply to studcnts’ ability to graduate with distinction.
Second, many students logically assume that the transcript-listed QPA determines eligibility --
the fact that it does not is confusing and engenders hard feelings in soon-to-be-alumni.
We ask the Faculty Senate to consider eliminating the sentence in s8.22.40 *Distinction*
that specifies the QPA for graduating with distinction is calculated using all courses attempted at
URI. Its deletion would mean that student eligibility for graduating cum/ magna/summa laude
would by default be determined using the transcript-listed QPA. This would eliminate student
confusion over their eligibility and ensure that the forgiveness embodied in the SGO and
conditional readmission policies applies throughout a student's time at the university.

3.30.18 Accelerated Bachelor's and Master's Degrees (ABM). Application
and Admission. Students applying for admission into ABM must do so
through the URI Graduate School admission system. Applicants must have
earned at least 75 credits before they are eligible to apply. Students will be
enrolled in ABM after they have met all Graduate School admission
requirements, and completed 90 undergraduate credits.
3.30.19 Credit Requirements. Only students accepted into the ABM program
will be able to double count credits towards both the bachelor's and master's
degrees. The total number of credits that will be allowed to be double
counted is up to one-third of the total credits required in the master's
program. Only 500-level courses and 400-level courses designated for
graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.
3.30.20 Credits Taken Outside of a program or from another department.
Students can transfer credits between URI programs and departments. Only
credits earned at URI may be counted toward the master's portion of the
ABM.
3.30.21 Time-to-degree Limit. Students must complete all graduate degree
requirements for an ABM within the time limit designated by the Graduate
School.
3.30.22 Proposals for New ABM Programs. Proposals for new ABM
Programs should be submitted to the Faculty Senate Curriculum and
Standards Committee after securing approval from the College in which the
ABM will be housed. Upon approval of the Curriculum and Standards
Committee, the proposal will be forward to the Graduate School. The New
Program Committee of the Graduate Council will review the proposal and
make a recommendation on its merits to the full Graduate Council. If
approved by vote of the Graduate Council, it will be submitted to the Faculty
Senate for review and approval as a joint Curriculum and Standards and
Graduate Council report.

The Thanatology minor (THN) has been very popular at the University since 1998. Over
the past two decades there have been major advances in the field, including a shift to
living with serious illness as well as end of life care. Current approaches, such as
palliative care, expand the scope to address these advances and reflect contemporary
practice for healthcare delivery. Thus, the curriculum needs to be updated to reflect
these advances. The College of Nursing would like to suspend entry into the THN
minor so we can evaluate currently approved classes and their ability to expand into a
palliative care lens and develop 1-2 new classes for a minor in Palliative Care.
This suspension will not impact students currently enrolled in the minor.

5.52.10 The President's Executive Council is a core team of university senior leaders tasked with
addressing pressing and long-term issues, immediate risks and opportunities, and strategic priority setting.
5.52.11 Members of the President's Executive Council may change from time to time, but generally include at
minimum Provost/Vice President for Academic Affairs, Vice President for Administration and Finance,
General Counsel, and the Senior Advisor and Chief of Staff to the President.
5.53.10 The President's Leadership Council is a collaborative leadership team focused on policy
deliberation and development, strategic implementation, and is responsible for excellence in overall University
operations.
5.53.11 Members of the President's Leadership Council may change from time to time, but generally include
Provost/Vice President for Academic Affairs, Vice President for Administration and Finance, Vice President
for Student Affairs, Vice President for Research and Economic Development, Associate Vice President &
Chief Diversity Officer, Executive Director for External Relations and Communications, Assistant Vice
President for Human Resources, General Counsel, President of URI Foundation and Alumni Relations,
Associate Vice President for Enrollment Management and Student Success, Chief Information Officer,
Director of Athletics, and Senior Advisor and Chief of Staff to the President.
5.54.10 The President's University Stewardship Council is composed of the University's academic and
administrative leaders responsible for purposeful information sharing, effective and inclusive decision-making,
clear and timely communications, and overall university stewardship.
5.54.11 Members of the President's University Stewardship Council may change from time to time, but will
include all members of the President's Leadership Council as well as the President of the Faculty Senate,
direct reports of the Provost/Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Directors of Legislative and
Government Relations, the Co-Directors of Budget, and the Deans of all academic schools/colleges,
including the deans of the Graduate School and of University Libraries.

Rationale:Academic excellence is a cornerstone value of the University of Rhode Island
and deserves appropriate recognition. Publication of the ^Dean's List', which each semester
recognizes undergraduate studentswho complete12 or more credits and earn a quality point
average of3.30 orhigher, serves as a crucialbenchmarkforincentivizing student success.An
increasing number of students,however, consistently exceed the quality point average
expectations set by the current ‘Dean's List’ and achieve significantly higher academic
performance. We believe that establishing a‘President's List’ that functions in a manner similar
to theDean's List but recognizesstudents eachsemester who complete12 ormore credits for a
letter grade and achieve a 3.80 quality point average, would provide distinct recognition for
students demonstrating exceptional academic performance. This recognition would incentivize
academic excellence and distinguish the highest-performing students. Several public R1 peer
institutions in New England have similar thresholds for superior academic achievement:
University of Maine (Dean’s: 3.5 GPA; President's: 3.8 GPA)
University of Massachusetts Dartmouth (Dean's: 3.2 GPA; Chancellor's: 3.8 GPA)
University of Massachusetts Lowell (Dean’s: 3.5 GPA; Chancellor's: 3.85 GPA)
University of New Hampshire (Dean's: 3.5 GPA; Dean's Highest Honors: 3.85 GPA)
The following legislation establishes a President's List at the University of Rhode Island.

describe the criteriafor‘Dean’s List'inthefirst sentence of8.57.10.EvanPreisser,Faculty
Senate Vice President, proposes removing the words “certain levels of' so that the first sentence
of 8.57.10 reads: *"Undergraduate students who achieved academic excellence.."

taking classes in the spring 2026 semester would be eligible for the ^President's List' designation

The graduate certificate in Prevention Science and Human Development is a fully online, stackable professional program that
will prepare students for a range of human services and health-related positions across a variety of sectors, particularly those
related to lifespan development, health promotion, and disease prevention such as program development and evaluation,
applied health research methods, social justice and health equity, and community engagement and advocacy.
The certificate is 12 credits: HDF511, HDF513, HDF533, and HDF536.

health and healthy development. There is an emphasis on examining social determinants of health with the aim of
enhancing equity and decreasing disparities. Additionally, this program provides intellectual development and training to a
This certificate can be completed to meet requirements in the Master's of Professional Studies program, the Master's of
Public Administration program, and the Master's of Public Health. For the Master's of Professional Studies (30 credits total),
students complete two certificates, and six additional credits of coursework. The Prevention Science certificate can be
the third certificate the students complete towards their degree. The certificate could also be taken as a stand-alone

required to these students. Therefore, having this certificate as an credential for the ABM-HDF students is imperative for

Rationale
The proposed Doctor of Education (Ed.D.) addresses an urgent and growing need for advanced educational leaders who can
respond to the complexities of today's learning environments.Across K-12 schools, higher education institutions,nonprofit
organizations, government agencies, and corporate learning settings, professionals are increasingly called upon to lead
change, implement evidence-based solutions, and advance equity in diverse contexts. The Ed.D. program will prepare
scholar-practitioners to investigate complex problems of practice,synthesize diverseforms of evidence,and generate
actionable solutions that improve learning and organizational outcomes.
The program aligns closely with the mission of the University of Rhode Island, which emphasizes high-quality education,
Education,the Ed.D. will develop leaders who embody these commitments by applying cutting-edge research and
implementation science to real-world educational issues in Rhode Island, across New England, and beyond.
The delivery model is designed for experienced professionals who are balancing advanced study with ongoing leadership
responsibilities. All core Ed.D. courses willbe delivered fully online, providing flexibility and accessibility to working
professionals across the region. Applied focus courses may be offered either online or in person, allowing students to tailor
their learning experience to their interests and professional needs. This modality supports the program's outcomes by
enabling candidates to remain embedded in their professional contexts while directly applying theory and evidence to
practice.

The Doctor of Education (Ed.D.) program provides graduates with a highly valued credential that prepares them for
advancement into mid- and senior-level leadership roles across a wide range of educational and organizational contexts. In
K-12 education and higher education, most leadership positions beyond the entry level require an advanced degree, with the
doctorate often serving as the preferred or distinguishing qualification.
Graduates of the Ed.D. will be well-positioned to pursue opportunities such as:
·District- and state-level leadership roles in K-12 education.
·Administrative and senior staff positions in colleges and universities.
·Leadership roles in nonprofit organizations focused on education, equity, and community development.
·Training, learning, and organizational development positions in industry and corporate settings.
but also to serve as consultants, policy advocates, and change agents who can influence educational practice and policy at
local, state, and national levels.

Engineering (BME) to become a standalone department, as well as the request for a department
name change should the proposal be approved.
On September 8, 2025, the Department of Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering
(ECBE) convened a faculty meeting. A total of 22 faculty members participated in the vote. Of
these, 20 were present in person, while two faculty members, who were unable to attend due to
scheduling conflicts, cast their votes remotely during the meeting time. In addition, you and
Professor Emeritus Ramada Kumaresan attended the meeting as non-voting participants.
The faculty unanimously supported the following actions:
(a) Initiating the process to seek approval for the Biomedical Engineering program to become
(b) Renaming the current ECBE department as the Department of Electrical and Computer
Engineering (ECE), contingent upon the establishment of BME as a separate department.
This decision was based on the vision for the future Biomedical Engineering department and
the department-level resource allocation plan presented during the meeting.
Thank you for your continued leadership and support as we take this important step toward
advancing the college's long-term vision. This collective faculty decision reflects our readiness
to support the next stages of the process under your guidance.
Professor and Chair, Electrical, Computer, and Biomedical Engineering

5a2db99c2035eefc2a847a4167e8b85fd0d4cfed: PROPOSED ALIGNMENT OF ACADEMIC CALENDARS
Academic Calendar Committee Report #2024-2025-03
April 10, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting
Rationale: When the URI Accelerated Online program began offering courses in seven-week
sessions, neither the two seven-week sessions in the fall nor the two seven-week sessions in the
spring were aligned with the start of URI's fall and spring semester. The resulting differences
between the Academic and Accelerated Online calendars had several unexpected consequences.
First, faculty who wished to teach in the Accelerated Online program could not do so as part of
their AY workload. Second, some sources of financial aid linked to the Academic calendar were
not available to students taking Accelerated Online courses. Third, students were prevented from
taking courses in-person, full seinester online, and accelerated online courses concurrently. As a
result, students are currently restricted to either classes that fall within the traditional calendar
OR Accelerated Online courses.
We propose changes to the University Mamual aligning the Academic and Accclerated Online
calendars. These changes are sufficient to address concerns (1) and (2), above. While they are
also necessary to address concern (3), additional legislation will be required to allow
calendar to simultaneously take online accelerated courses (and vice versa).

and some also require approval by the Board of Trustees; new courses and course

General Principles. The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) reviews
undergraduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 100-, 200-, 300-,
and 40o-levels, except in cases of General Education courses, for which the General
Education Committee (GEC) performs the review. The Graduate Council (GC) processes
graduate curriculum matters, including proposals for courses at the 400- (for graduate
credit), 500-, 600-, and 900-levels. If a proposal for a 400-level course indicates that it is
to be offered for graduate credit as well as undergraduate credit, it is processed by both
the respective undergraduate curriculum committee and the Graduate Council. These
review committees meet monthly and submit approved proposals to the Faculty Senate
for action (approval at a Faculty Senate meeting).
Part 2. Deadlines and Timeline.
In planning for the first offering of 1) a newly proposed course, or 2) the implementation
of major changes to an existing course or academic program, please be aware that the
review and approval of a proposal is a multi-step process that can take several months
and is not complete until the course/course change is officially listed in e-Campus or,
with regard to new programs, until approval has been received from the URI Board of
Trustees. All faculty have access to the Kuali Curriculum Management System for
submitting a new proposal, checking the status of an existing proposal, or viewing an
approved proposal. Questions regarding Kuali access and use should be directed to the
Faculty Senate office.
It is advisable to think 'a year ahead,' i.e., proposals for a fall-semester course should be
submitted early in the previous fall semester. This suggested timeline reflects the fact that
courses submitted at the end of the year-1 fall semester may not be listed in e-Campus
before student enrollment for the year-2 fall semester begins in the middle of the year-1
spring semester (see below). There may not be sufficient time for proposals submitted in
the spring to be fully approved before the end of the academic year (consult the Faculty
Senate website for important academic-year deadlines).
Fully approved course changes will be made in e-Campus for the subsequent semester
up to, but not after, the start of pre-registration for that semester (on or about mid-
semester). Pre-registration for the Spring semester starts in mid-October; pre-registration
for the Fall semester starts in early March. Contact Enrollment Services for exact dates.
Fully approved course changes to Learning Community courses for the subsequent
academic year will be made in e-Campus only up to the second week of February.
